0.text: Social phobia, or social anxiety disorder, is characterized by intense anxiety in social situations. Seeking help is one of the common situations that can trigger anxiety for people with this disorder.
0.fact: Charles Darwin, the famous naturalist and author of the theory of evolution, suffered from severe social phobia. Despite his outstanding achievements, he avoided public speaking and often experienced panic attacks when faced with the need to interact with others.

1.text: Glossophobia is the fear of public speaking, one of the most common forms of social phobia. About 75% of people experience some degree of fear when speaking in public.
1.fact: According to a survey by the American Psychological Association, about 30% of Americans experience a strong fear of public speaking, making it one of the most common fears.

2.text: A key aspect of social phobia is the fear of social interaction with strangers. This can manifest as avoiding contact, trying to remain unnoticed, or feeling awkward and anxious.
2.fact: Franz Kafka, the renowned writer, suffered from severe social phobia and often struggled to communicate with strangers. His works, such as “The Trial” and “The Castle,” reflect his deep-seated fears and anxieties.

3.text: People with social phobia often avoid phone calls and video conferences due to a fear of being misunderstood or making a bad impression. They may worry about how their voice sounds or what they might say.
3.fact: One way to reduce anxiety before phone calls is through practice and preparation. Creating a list of questions and answers before a call can help a person feel more confident and reduce fear.

4.text: Social phobia can lead people to avoid socializing outside of essential situations (such as work or school) to prevent potentially anxiety-inducing social interactions.
4.fact: Studies suggest that around 15 million Americans (about 7% of the population) live with social anxiety, and many of them prefer to stay away from social situations beyond their required roles.

5.text: Entering a crowded room can be particularly anxiety-inducing for people with social phobia due to the fear of being the center of attention. They may worry about being watched or judged.
5.fact: Albert Einstein, the great physicist, suffered from severe social phobia and avoided large gatherings. He preferred to work alone and only interacted with close friends and colleagues.

6.text: People with social phobia may be very sensitive to criticism, especially on social media, where it is public and can be seen by many people.
6.fact: Digital detoxing is becoming increasingly popular. Many people, including celebrities, temporarily disconnect from social media to restore their mental well-being and reduce the impact of negative criticism.

7.text: Silence can be a way to avoid negative attention and potential criticism, but it can also limit career growth and professional opportunities.
7.fact: Active listening techniques can help people feel more confident in meetings. For example, focusing on listening and preparing questions or comments in advance can help reduce anxiety and improve participation in discussions.

8.text: Social phobia is characterized by intense anxiety in situations where a person might be evaluated by others. One such situation is being asked to express an opinion in front of a group. This can trigger a fear of making a mistake or being judged negatively.

9.text: People with social phobia may experience intense anxiety and discomfort in crowded places, such as the subway. These environments can trigger a fear of being noticed, judged, or facing unexpected social situations.
9.fact: Adele, the well-known British singer, has spoken about her social anxiety and panic attacks. She avoids crowded places such as the underground to reduce the risk of intense anxiety symptoms.

10.text: People with social phobia often try to avoid being the center of attention to prevent drawing unnecessary interest or being judged by others. They may experience a fear of criticism or ridicule, which increases the desire to stay in the shadows.

11.text: According to the National Institute of Mental Health, about 12.1% of the population will experience social anxiety disorder in their lifetime, which often leads to the avoidance of public places.

12.text: Research shows that a moderate level of anxiety can actually improve performance by activating the sympathetic nervous system and increasing focus. This phenomenon is known as the Yerkes-Dodson law.

13.text: Anxiety regarding social interaction is known as “social anxiety” and can range from mild discomfort to intense fear. It is the third most common mental disorder, after depression and alcohol use disorder.

14.text: The fear of authority figures has its own name — “hierarchophobia.” While not an official medical term, it is often used to describe excessive anxiety when interacting with people in higher positions.
14.fact: Warren Buffett, one of the world’s most successful investors, experienced a strong fear of public speaking and interacting with authority figures in his youth. He even took a course to overcome this fear, which later significantly helped his career.

15.text: Fear of going to shopping malls may be linked to agoraphobia — the fear of open spaces or places where it is difficult to find an exit quickly. However, it can also be a manifestation of social phobia or ochlophobia (fear of crowds).

16.text: Psychologists call the fear of the unknown “intolerance of uncertainty.” This state can affect not only social situations but also decision-making in general.

17.text: The fear of speaking before an unfamiliar audience is called “social evaluative anxiety.” This is a combination of the fear of negative evaluation and the fear of new situations.
17.fact: Oscar winner Emma Stone has spoken openly about her struggle with panic attacks, especially in situations involving performing before a new audience. She has used therapy and breathing techniques to cope.

18.text: The fear of making phone calls is known as “telephonophobia.” This phenomenon is becoming increasingly common in the digital age, as people become more accustomed to text-based communication.
18.fact: A study conducted by BankMyCell in 2019 showed that 76% of millennials feel anxiety when they need to make a phone call. Among Gen Z, this figure is even higher — 81%.

19.text: Anxiety when returning items may be linked to a fear of conflict, fear of negative evaluation, or feeling guilty about “inconveniencing” store staff.
19.fact: Anxiety during product returns is often linked to a broader phenomenon known as “assertiphobia” — the fear of standing up for one’s rights or expressing one’s needs.

20.text: The fear of unprepared speaking is often linked to “imposter syndrome” — the feeling that you are not competent enough and might be “exposed.”
20.fact: “Improvisational thinking” can be a helpful technique. Instead of panicking about a lack of preparation, try to view the situation as an opportunity for spontaneous and sincere communication with your audience.

21.text: The fear of writing or taking notes in the presence of others is sometimes called “scriptophobia.” This is a specific form of social anxiety related to the fear of being judged by those around you.
21.fact: There is no precise data on the prevalence of this fear, but a study published in the Journal of Anxiety Disorders showed that about 7% of people experience significant discomfort when they need to write in the presence of others.

22.text: Psychologists call the difficulty of saying no, especially to persistent people, “people-pleasing syndrome.” This is linked to a desire to avoid conflict and a fear of negative evaluation.
22.fact: A study by the University of Pennsylvania showed that about 68% of people feel discomfort when they need to say “no” in sales situations.

23.text: Martin Luther King Jr., the renowned civil rights leader, experienced intense anxiety when expressing his opinions before groups early in his career. However, by overcoming his fears, he became one of the most influential orators and leaders of the human rights movement.

24.text: People with social anxiety may experience intense anxiety and stress when receiving unexpected invitations to weddings or other celebrations. Such events often involve interacting with many people, which can be particularly challenging for them.
24.fact: Daniel Radcliffe, known for his role as Harry Potter, experiences social phobia and often avoids large public events. He prefers spending time in small groups of friends and family.

25.text: People with social phobia often avoid phone calls in the presence of others due to a fear of being heard and judged. They may worry about how their voice sounds, potential slips of the tongue, or that their conversation might trigger a negative reaction from those around them.

26.text: Avoiding parties can be linked to “safety behaviors” — strategies that reduce anxiety in the short term but may increase social isolation and fear in the long run.

27.text: Research shows that about 7–9% of people suffer from paruresis, also known as shy bladder syndrome, which causes them to avoid using public restrooms.

28.text: People with social phobia may feel intense anxiety when receiving invitations for meetings or dates. Common reasons include fear of negative evaluation, self-doubt, and worry about potential social blunders.

29.text: Fear of phone calls, especially from unknown numbers, can be caused by anxiety over not knowing how to respond correctly or worrying that the conversation might not go as expected. This may include a fear of potential confrontation or the need to react quickly to unexpected questions.

30.text: People with social phobia may experience significant anxiety when interacting with strangers while traveling or on vacation. They might fear negative evaluation, worry about doing something inappropriate, or not know how to keep a conversation going.

31.text: Studies show that about 60% of people with social anxiety experience discomfort with eye contact. This can be one of the most anxiety-inducing aspects of social interaction.

32.text: People with social phobia may experience intense anxiety at the prospect of conflict or arguments with strangers. They may fear negative evaluation, being misunderstood, or even an aggressive reaction, leading them to avoid any potentially conflict-prone situations.

33.text: Research indicates that about 20–30% of people experience significant discomfort when being photographed, especially in groups. This anxiety may be linked to a fear of negative evaluation and dissatisfaction with their appearance.

34.text: Isaac Newton, the great scientist, was also very reclusive and avoided public events and new groups. He preferred to spend his time alone conducting scientific research.

35.text: Research shows that cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) can be highly effective in treating social anxiety. CBT helps people change unhelpful thoughts and develop a more positive attitude toward social interactions.

36.text: Anxiety regarding practical skills exams is a common issue, especially for those with social phobia. The fear of being evaluated and the possibility of failure can intensify stress and nervousness.
36.fact: Thomas Edison, the famous inventor, struggled with traditional learning methods and exams. He preferred learning through practical experiments and trials, avoiding formal testing.

37.text: People with social phobia often experience intense anxiety during conversations with others. The fear of negative evaluation, worry about how their words will be perceived, and the fear of making a mistake can heighten anxiety and nervousness.

38.text: People with social phobia often prefer to walk during hours when there are few or no people on the streets. This helps them avoid social interactions that might trigger anxiety and stress.
38.fact: Howard Hughes, the famous American businessman and aviator known for his social phobia and multiple phobias, preferred solitary walks and avoided crowded places. He tried to remain inconspicuous and avoid social interactions.

39.text: Eye contact activates mirror neurons, which can enhance feelings of empathy and understanding, but can also trigger strong emotions. This may be one reason why eye contact causes such anxiety.

normal.text: Your results show that you feel confident in most social situations. Interacting with strangers, participating in discussions, or speaking in front of an audience typically doesn’t cause you significant discomfort. This suggests that you can interact freely with others and feel comfortable in social settings.
normal.title: No signs of social anxiety

mild.text: Your answers suggest that you may feel tension or uncertainty in certain social situations. Interacting with strangers, public speaking, or being the center of attention can be stressful for you. This is a very common experience, and with support and practice, your self-confidence can significantly grow.
mild.title: Mild social anxiety

moderate.text: Your results show that social situations can cause you significant anxiety and discomfort. This may affect your self-confidence and your desire to connect with others. These experiences can be very exhausting, but with support and a willingness to work through them, it is possible to gradually reduce your anxiety and feel more at ease in social interactions.
moderate.title: Severe social anxiety

text: How comfortable do you feel in social situations? Feeling anxious when communicating, meeting new people, or speaking in public is a very common reaction.

This test will help you better understand your relationship with social interactions and your potential level of social anxiety. Recognizing your reactions is an important step toward building confidence and feeling calmer in social settings.
